aberdeen-free-haircuts.kidSummary: Barbers in Aberdeen, Mississippi, used their fall break to cut students' hair for free. A local station reported about 100 haircuts, so children could go back to class feeling looked after. At one shop, students were still in the chairs ahead of Monday. A student in a chair said the barbers were using their own break for kids who could not afford a cut. A community volunteer said it was kindness toward people the barbers did not already know. The report stops at the chairs and the reason. It does not list a sign-up for a repeat event.
kidQuestions: Why might a haircut change how a student feels about going back to school?
What is the difference between helping someone you know and someone you do not?
What is one skill you could share with another student?

aiea-sugar-mill-park.kidSummary: Thirty-four trees are now growing where an old sugar mill stood in ʻAiea, Hawaiʻi. They are the first step toward a community park. The city supplied the trees with a grant of $34,000. The mix includes milo, wiliwili, and a Moreton Bay fig. Schools, civic clubs, and other partners helped put them in the ground. A neighborhood group is leading the plan to turn the mill site into a park. The trees are a start. The park itself is not finished yet.
kidQuestions: Why might a neighborhood plant trees before a park is finished?
Which tree in the mix would you want to learn more about?
How could a class help care for young trees?

argyle-little-library.kidSummary: A 4-H club called Dog Gone Kids opened a Little Free Library in Argyle, New York. It stands outside the Cornell Cooperative Extension office on Main Street. It is the club's third book box in Washington County. Grandparents built it, and a hardware store set the post in concrete. Anyone may take a book or leave one. The club collected books for children and adults over the summer and plans to keep the box stocked. The office has asked neighbors for cookbooks and magazines, and it has asked them to skip old encyclopedias and outdated books.
kidQuestions: How does a sidewalk book box work if there is no librarian?
Why might a club ask people not to leave certain books?
What book would you leave for a younger child?

asheville-swannanoa.kidSummary: A dam on the Swannanoa River near Asheville broke open in a hurricane, and fish used the gap. Smallmouth bass and russet darters have been found upstream of the dam for the first time in more than a hundred years. Scientists and a college are the ones who found them. The city will not rebuild the barrier, so the fish can keep swimming through. This is early news about two kinds of fish. It is not a full list of everything living in the river, and the river is still healing.
kidQuestions: Why would a broken dam be good news for a fish?
What is the difference between finding two kinds of fish and saying a whole river is healthy?
What would you look for if you visited this river with a class?

aspen-snowmass-snow-storage.kidSummary: In Colorado, a ski resort piled up spring snow and covered it with insulated blankets. After a dry winter and a summer of drought records, about 85 percent of the snow stored at Snowmass was still there, and about 84 percent was left at Buttermilk. The resort says making that much snow from scratch would have taken about 3.5 million gallons of water. One weekend, people skied on a short run built from the saved snow. The resort has already bought more blankets. Saving snow may mean less water and energy spent making new snow later.
kidQuestions: How can a blanket help a pile of snow last through summer?
Why does saving snow also save water?
What would you measure if you checked the pile at the end of summer?

atlanta-cp-soccer.kidSummary: An occupational therapist in Georgia started a soccer team after a patient said he wanted to play. CP Soccer Atlanta gives children with cerebral palsy a side of their own. Eight-year-old goalie Tayden Merrell said it means he is not alone. The team is a place to play. It is not a medical treatment, and it does not change a diagnosis. What it changes is the chance to be on a field with other children who understand the game the way he plays it. World Cup events for the sport were scheduled in Fayetteville, Georgia.
kidQuestions: Why did it matter that a patient said he wanted to play?
How can a team help someone feel less alone?
What rule would you change so more children could join a game?

bangor-petal-it-forward.kidSummary: A flower shop in Bangor, Maine, stood in West Market Square and gave flowers to strangers. It was the shop's fifth year in a national day called Petal It Forward. Each person got two stems: one to keep and one to hand to someone else. The office manager said she likes the moment people realize the flower is free, and that some of them cry or hug her. Bangor Floral was one of seven Maine shops that day, among more than 700 across the country. The shop called it one way to give back to a city that has kept them in business for more than a century.
kidQuestions: Why give two flowers instead of one?
How can a small free gift change a stranger's day?
Who would you hand the second flower to, and why?

basking-ridge-foodstock.kidSummary: Three students at Ridge High School in Basking Ridge, New Jersey, ran the town's first Foodstock. Elise Asay, Cole Marshall, and Nicole Zenchak had volunteers hand out bags door to door in August and ask neighbors to fill them with unopened food that would not spoil. All 3,200 pounds went to the county food bank. The drive ended with a backyard music festival the three students hosted. They hope the collection and the festival become a yearly town event. A wider Foodstock effort has collected more than 1.5 million pounds of food across New Jersey.
kidQuestions: Why ask neighbors to fill a bag instead of buying all the food yourselves?
What kinds of food are useful to a food bank, and what kinds are not?
How could your class run a smaller version of this drive?

bena-leech-lake-reading.kidSummary: Bug-O-Nay-Ge-Shig School, on the Leech Lake Reservation in Bena, Minnesota, spent two years on a structured reading program. In that time, students made close to four years of progress in basic reading skills. Some older students who had been three or four grades behind are now reading on grade level. The gain is in those basic skills, for the students the school measured. It comes from two years of the same program. It is not a claim about every class in the building. It is a clear result from sticking with one way of teaching.
kidQuestions: What does two years of practice make possible that one week cannot?
Why does it matter to say which students were measured?
What helps you keep going when reading feels hard?

bentonville-crystal-bridges.kidSummary: Crystal Bridges Museum in Bentonville, Arkansas, opened an outdoor playscape called the Ozark Discovery Canopy. Visitors can splash in a creek, turn a large boulder, lounge on oversized hanging benches, and race down a wide slide big enough for a family. The museum says it is not a traditional playground. It sits with the campus trails and outdoor art, and it is open from dawn to dusk every day. The opening follows a major expansion of the museum earlier this year. The playscape is a place to play that is also a place to look at the woods.
kidQuestions: How is this playscape different from a playground with swings and a slide only?
Why might a museum want children playing outside as well as looking at art?
What would you build first if you designed an outdoor play space?

billings-river-cleanup.kidSummary: Volunteers in Montana set a record on the Yellowstone River. On one September day, 165 people on shore and in 30 boats pulled 17,100 pounds of trash from the water. The haul included 191 tires. The biggest tire weighed 1,445 pounds. Crews also found three engine blocks and sent 75,328 pounds of metal to be recycled. The whole project took 3,277 hours of work, counting the wider cleanup. The river is cleaner by that much. The organizers say the job is not finished.
kidQuestions: Why is a tire in a river a problem for the animals that live there?
What could a class do to keep trash from reaching a river near you?
Why might metal from the river be recycled instead of thrown away?

birmingham-victory-day.kidSummary: At a high school in Birmingham, Michigan, halftime of a powderpuff game became Victory Day. Middle and high school students with cognitive and physical impairments played football or cheered, each paired with a player or cheerleader from the school. The program started 16 years ago in another Michigan town after a teacher's idea, and it now reaches dozens of districts. The coach said it gives Special Olympics athletes a moment in the sun and builds empathy in the school. For one evening, the field belonged to students who do not always get that spotlight.
kidQuestions: What does it feel like to be cheered for in front of a crowd?
How might playing beside someone change what a team notices?
What is one way your school could share the field more fairly?

blandings-turtles-great-meadows.kidSummary: Schoolchildren in Massachusetts helped endangered Blanding's turtles at Great Meadows in Concord. A news report said the number of adult turtles has climbed from about 55 to about 300. Students gave the turtles a head start, and the numbers are moving in the right direction. The turtles are still rare. The report does not spell out every step of the classroom work. It does establish the marsh, the students' help, and a population that is larger than it was.
kidQuestions: What does it mean to give a baby turtle a head start?
Why do you think students, not only scientists, were part of this work?
How would you explain an endangered animal to a younger child?

bloomington-kitten-aquarium.kidSummary: About two dozen foster kittens from a rescue group walked through an underwater tunnel at an aquarium in the Mall of America in Bloomington, Minnesota. Sharks and rays swam overhead. The group does this once a year to help kittens get used to new sights and gentle handling before they are adopted. These are orphaned foster cats, not aquarium animals. The rescue is caring for about 1,000 kittens this year. A strange room can make a young cat braver around people. The bigger job is still the daily care of the much larger group.
kidQuestions: Why might a new place help a kitten get ready for a home?
How is a foster kitten different from an animal that lives at the aquarium?
What would you do to help a shy kitten feel safe?

bucksport-veteran-cards.kidSummary: Evan Hunter, who is 10, got his mother and 27 volunteers together in Bucksport, Maine, and wrote thank-you cards to veterans. They filled out 1,100 of them on a Saturday. The family has held the same writing day every year since 2020. The cards are notes, not a big program. The count is how many they finished in that one sitting, with the same neighbors coming back each year. A short message, written by hand, was the whole gift.
kidQuestions: Why might a handwritten note matter to someone who served?
How does doing the same kind project every year change it?
What would you write in a thank-you card that is only a few sentences?

butcherknife-creek.kidSummary: Butcherknife Creek runs beside an elementary school in Steamboat Springs, Colorado. A charitable trust and local fly fishers rebuilt the stream so trout have better habitat. Middle and high school students are already using it as an outdoor classroom. The idea started with two teachers who fish. They wanted a living stream right outside the door, where students could watch how a creek works. The project is finished, not still a drawing. Students can study a real fishery without leaving the school grounds.
kidQuestions: What could you learn from a creek that you could not learn from a picture of one?
Why might trout need a restored stream instead of a straight ditch?
If your school had an outdoor classroom, what should it be?

cape-neddick-red-bat.kidSummary: An Eastern red bat was found struggling in the waves on a beach in Maine. Rescuers took the bat to the Center for Wildlife in Cape Neddick. The bat was very tired and barely moving on arrival. Now the bat is active and eating mealworms. A good appetite is a sign this bat is recovering. Eastern red bats are one of eight kinds of bats in southern Maine. This story is about one animal getting stronger. It does not say how all the bats along the coast are doing.
kidQuestions: Why is eating again a good sign for a rescued animal?
What should a person do if they find a bat that needs help?
How is one rescued bat different from a count of a whole species?

chiefland-sinkhole-dog.kidSummary: A border collie in Chiefland, Florida, fell into a sinkhole about 10 feet deep and was stuck from 5 in the morning. Neighbors stayed with the rescue. A concrete contractor brought a small digging machine. Firefighters and county road crews dug too. When the hole was open enough, the dog jumped into her owners' arms. No single team did the job alone. It took ordinary tools and people who did not leave. The story is about a dog getting home, and about neighbors who kept digging.
kidQuestions: Why did it take more than one group to free the dog?
How would you help if a neighbor's animal was in trouble?
What is a sinkhole, and why can it be dangerous?

cincinnati-gelato-kitten.kidSummary: Shelter staff in Cincinnati built a tiny wheelchair from Hot Wheels cars and rulers for a stray kitten named Gelato, who has a back injury. A tattoo artist named Hope Hollandsworth adopted him to live with her other cats who need extra care. The report does not give the shelter's formal name. It also does not say Gelato is cured, and it does not spell out a long medical future. What it does report is the handmade wheelchair and the adoption. A small invention gave one kitten a way to move, and a home.
kidQuestions: How can a simple wheelchair change a kitten's day?
Why is it important not to say Gelato is cured if the report does not say that?
What is one way to include an animal that moves differently?

cincinnati-manatee-calves.kidSummary: An orphaned manatee calf named Hundo left the Cincinnati Zoo heavier and stronger than when he arrived. He came in at about 150 pounds and left weighing 546 pounds, headed for more care in Florida before a winter release. Three more orphaned calves then moved into the zoo's Manatee Springs: Tuglet, Smidge, and Zimomo. Each was rescued at a little over 40 pounds and now weighs more than 350. They are still in care. They are not back in the wild yet. Keepers said they are ready to start the calves' rehab.
kidQuestions: Why do orphaned manatee calves need people before they can live in the ocean?
What does a big weight gain tell you about Hundo?
Why is it too early to say the three new calves are ready for the wild?

cobb-county-puppies.kidSummary: Firefighters at a station in Cobb County, Georgia, had just finished training on how to care for pets. Then a veterinary clinic called. A dog needed an emergency birth, and the clinic wanted help. The crew cleared the newborn puppies' airways, gave medicine, and moved them into incubators. Fifteen puppies were delivered on that one shift. The training was new. The clinic called because the birth could not wait. The report is about that call. It does not say every firefighter now delivers puppies.
kidQuestions: Why did the practice the firefighters had just finished matter that day?
What does an incubator do for a newborn puppy?
How is helping one litter different from saying a whole county is trained?

coeur-dalene-trivia-lunches.kidSummary: Leah Weber, a 10-year-old in Coeur d'Alene, Idaho, won $500 at a football game by answering a potato-themed trivia question, with the crowd helping. She did not know her class would be surprised with the check. She had already decided to give all of it to her school so families who cannot afford lunch can still eat. She had written the principal to say that was the plan. She told the paper she has a friend without much money and does not want anyone to miss lunch. Her classmates applauded.
kidQuestions: Why did Leah give the prize away instead of keeping it?
What happens at school when a student cannot pay for lunch?
If you won $500, what need in your school would you want to meet?

columbus-second-grade-library.kidSummary: Every second-grader in Columbus, Ohio, is getting a free field trip to the Main Library. The trips started at Liberty Elementary with stories, songs, and dancing in the children's area. Students used cards that work as library cards to check out books, and they went home with backpacks. Nearly 4,500 second-graders at 79 elementary schools are included. A library foundation is paying for the buses and the program. The library's leader called second grade a critical year for learning to read. The superintendent said she wants students curious enough to come back on their own.
kidQuestions: Why might second grade be an important year for reading?
What would you want to find on a first trip to a big library?
How is a library card different from borrowing a book from a friend?

common-good-city-farm.kidSummary: Common Good City Farm sits on a former baseball field in Washington, D.C. It grows about 4,500 pounds of fruits and vegetables a year. At its market, people can take up to $30 worth of produce whether or not they can pay. The farm said that saved customers about $20,000 last year. A fridge and pantry outside the gates stay stocked with rescued food, about 6,000 pounds so far. The farm also accepts food benefits, trains adults in regenerative farming, and hires about 25 teenagers each summer. This fall it planned a free family Halloween celebration and a turkey and grocery giveaway.
kidQuestions: Why let people take food even when they cannot pay?
What is rescued food, and why would a farm give it away?
How could teenagers working on a farm help a neighborhood?

conway-float-with-flame.kidSummary: Conway, Arkansas, held its first Float with the Flame, a swim relay that raised $5,610 for Special Olympics of Arkansas. More than 100 people took part, from 8-year-olds to college students and local first responders. They carried a torch through the pool at the community center. A college team won the first champion title. Emergency squad members swam too, and one said their usual work is swift water, a different kind of swimming, and that they plan to come back next year. The day put Special Olympics at the center of a town pool.
kidQuestions: What does it mean to carry a torch for someone else's team?
Why might first responders want to swim in a race like this?
How can a sport include people of many ages and abilities?

denver-zoo-white-rhinos.kidSummary: The Denver Zoo has southern white rhinos for the first time in 130 years. Two young males, Mkuu and Viazi, came from zoos in Tampa. Their names mean prince and potatoes. Both are males, so this is not a breeding pair and not a birth announcement. Zoos move rhinos among accredited parks to keep a healthy population in human care. Southern white rhinos are still threatened in the wild. What changed in Denver is that these two animals now live there, where keepers can care for them.
kidQuestions: Why would zoos move animals from one city to another?
Why doesn't this arrival mean baby rhinos are on the way?
What is the difference between an animal in a zoo and one in the wild?

effingham-little-library.kidSummary: A little free library now sits outside the sheriff's office in Springfield, Georgia, in Effingham County. Anyone can take a book or leave one, at no cost. Volunteer Amanda West led the project. She said she wanted the box because reading builds empathy and gives people a free escape. The sheriff said he hopes children and families will use it. The box is registered with Little Free Library, the nonprofit that supports neighborhood book exchanges. It is a small library that does not need a card or a due date.
kidQuestions: How can a book help someone understand another person?
Why put a library where families already walk by?
What book would you leave in a box for a stranger?

evergreen-park-cockatiel.kidSummary: Daniel Kirincic, a high school sophomore in Evergreen Park, Illinois, had wanted a cockatiel for years. On his 15th birthday he was walking to cross-country practice when a bright yellow bird sat on the track bleachers. It was calm around people, and it looked like a cockatiel he had painted in art class the year before. His mother brought a net, they got the bird home, and she found the owner online. The owner said Daniel could keep it. The bird's name is Tico.
kidQuestions: How did Daniel's art project help him notice the bird?
Why was it important to look for the owner before keeping Tico?
What would you do if you found a pet that seemed lost?

forks-little-library.kidSummary: Forks, Washington, has a new little free library on Spartan Avenue, in front of a church. The box is stocked and open for anyone to take a book or leave one. Children's titles are a focus, and one neighbor added homemade bookmarks. Several people were thanked for building it. It is a sidewalk library, the kind a neighbor can use without a card or a due date. The whole idea is small on purpose: a box, some books, and a rule that anyone may share.
kidQuestions: Why focus a little library on children's books?
What makes a homemade bookmark a useful gift with a book?
How would you help keep a sidewalk library stocked?

front-royal-cheetah-cubs.kidSummary: Five cheetah cubs were born on October 5 at a Smithsonian conservation center in Front Royal, Virginia. Their mother, Zura, is five and raising cubs for the first time. The cubs are healthy. They started climbing on her the day they were born. Staff are staying out of the den and watching on a camera. The campus is closed to visitors, so a live camera is how the public can see them. This is the center's 21st cheetah litter. The cubs were born with their eyes and ears closed, which is normal for newborns.
kidQuestions: Why are the keepers staying out of the den?
What can a camera show that a crowd of visitors might disturb?
What do you notice about how a newborn cheetah is different from an adult?

goshen-trojan-shoes.kidSummary: Football players from Troy University visited Goshen Elementary School in Alabama with new shoes and hats. They partnered with a hat company and the nonprofit Shoes That Fit. It is the second year those three partners have done this together for the school. The news report is short. It does not say how many students received shoes, what sizes were offered, or what the visit cost. It does say the team came back. College players, a shoe nonprofit, and a store showed up again with new shoes and hats for elementary students.
kidQuestions: Why might new shoes matter on a school day?
Why is it useful to know what the report does not say?
What is a gift you could give that helps someone join an activity?

granby-animal-shelter.kidSummary: Grand County, Colorado, has a new animal shelter in Granby. The old building was too small because the county had grown. Neighbors and viewers of a local news station donated thousands of dollars. At a weekend celebration, people who helped pay for the building cut a leash instead of a ribbon. Staff were still moving in. The doors were set to open to the public on October 1. The sheriff said the shelter shows what a county can do when people work together to care for its animals.
kidQuestions: Why did the county need a bigger shelter?
How is cutting a leash a fitting way to open an animal shelter?
What would you want a shelter to have so animals feel safe?

greensboro-horse-logger.kidSummary: In Greensboro, Vermont, John Smolinsky still hauls logs with a horse. His Belgian horse, Ted, weighs about a ton. They work on small woodlots that are steep or easy to damage. Horse logging is a Vermont craft about 200 years old. A horse lifts its feet, so it packs the soil much less than a heavy machine does. That difference is why Ted still goes into woods where a big skidder would leave a deeper mark. The work is slow, and it is chosen on purpose.
kidQuestions: Why can a horse be gentler on a forest than a heavy machine?
What kind of woods would you choose a horse for?
What is one old way of working that you think is still worth keeping?

hallsville-book-vending.kidSummary: Hallsville West Elementary in Texas has given students more than 1,000 books through a vending machine in the main hallway. A grant paid for the machine five years ago, when the school opened. Students earn a book by being named student of the month for good habits. Each month, 38 students, one from each class, pick a title after an assembly. The librarian said that pace, on a campus of nearly 700 students, is what carried the machine to 1,000 books. Teachers and a library aide were credited along with the years of funding.
kidQuestions: How is earning a book different from buying one?
Why give the choice of the book to the student?
What habit at school do you think is worth celebrating?

hastings-harvey-greeter.kidSummary: Five-year-old Harvey Wetterlund walks through Hastings, Minnesota, saying hello. After his family moved from Washington state, the walks became a routine of hellos and hugs at the fire station, the police station, a coffee shop, and other stores. The mayor gave him a key to the city and named him an honorary greeter. She said kindness is free. Friends built him a child-sized chair painted with first-responder logos. A shop owner said Harvey yells hello to each mechanic by name, and it makes the day better. Harvey's advice is short: be a friend to everybody.
kidQuestions: How can a hello change someone's workday?
Why do you think adults wanted to honor a five-year-old?
Who in your town could use a friendly greeting?

hoboken-shelter-5k.kidSummary: Jacob Cyprys, a sixth grader in Hoboken, New Jersey, is the leading individual fundraiser for a shelter's yearly 5K. He has raised $1,780. Before his 12th birthday he asked neighbors for $12 each to help people facing hunger and housing trouble. He first ran in the shelter's kids' race in 2017, when he was three. This year he planned to run the full course with his mother after months of weekend training. He said he wants everyone to have a home. The shelter's director said the effort is a reminder that kindness has no age limit.
kidQuestions: Why might a small gift from many neighbors add up?
What does training for months say about how much Jacob cared?
How could a class help people who need food or a home, without spending much?

honolulu-marine-debris.kidSummary: A ship came home to Honolulu after cleaning a huge ocean reserve in Hawaiʻi. On this last voyage of a five-year project, crews removed 47,000 pounds of debris. More than half of it was old fishing nets stuck on coral. They also picked up nearly 3,000 pounds of plastic from shorelines and freed five green sea turtles caught in nets. Since 2020 the same project has removed more than 1.3 million pounds. Those bigger numbers are for the whole five years, not for this one trip. Back on shore, the debris will be sorted, recycled, or burned.
kidQuestions: Why are lost fishing nets dangerous for turtles and coral?
What is the difference between this one voyage and the five-year total?
What is one thing people can do so less plastic reaches the ocean?

i25-wildlife-overpass.kidSummary: A bridge for animals now crosses Interstate 25 near Castle Rock, Colorado. In the 10 months after it opened, drivers hit two animals on a stretch that used to see about one collision a day. That is a drop of 91 percent. Pronghorn crossed the highway on the bridge for the first time in decades. Six more crossings are being designed. The count is about crashes, not a promise that every animal in the area uses the bridge. It does show that a safe path over the road can keep both animals and drivers safer.
kidQuestions: Why is a bridge for animals safer than asking them to cross the lanes?
What does a 91 percent drop in crashes tell you?
Which wild animal near you would need a safe way across a road?

jackson-dampier-camp.kidSummary: Dozens of children from first through eighth grade spent a morning at a free basketball camp in Jackson, Mississippi. A former NBA player, Eric Dampier, was there with his son and other sports leaders. The camp was at a college gym. Organizers said the morning was for teamwork, time with Dampier, and moving around. It was one morning. It was not a tryout, and it was not a promise of a roster spot. The point was to play, to listen, and to practice being on a team.
kidQuestions: What can you learn from a camp that is not a tryout?
Why is teamwork a skill even if you never play on a big team?
Who in your community could teach you something they know well?

jeffco-nasa-hunch.kidSummary: Students in Jefferson County, Colorado, design and build hardware for NASA. Their district is one of only three in the country named a Center of Excellence in a program that links high schools with the space agency. They work on ideas astronauts have raised, for the space station and for Artemis missions aimed at the Moon. Some projects have already gone to the station for testing. On a Friday they reviewed the work with NASA mentors, a rare chance to get feedback before they improve it. Last year more than 30 projects from the program were picked to compete in Houston.
kidQuestions: What is different about building something that might go to space?
Why do mentors give feedback before a project is finished?
What problem at school would you want a team of students to solve?

jocko-fish-rescue.kidSummary: Crews restoring the Jocko River in Montana found fish stranded when water moved into a new channel. Workers from the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes collected hundreds of fish, including a cutthroat trout, and carried them in coolers to the new channel so they would not be left behind. The project is letting the river spread toward its floodplain again, instead of staying squeezed along a hillside. The rescue was one day in a longer repair. It does not mean the whole fishery is finished.
kidQuestions: Why did the fish need a ride to the new part of the river?
What is a floodplain, and why might a river need one?
How is one rescue day different from a finished river?

kansas-city-giving-grove.kidSummary: The Giving Grove started in Kansas City 14 years ago with a simple idea: plant fruit trees and let people pick for free. Volunteers now count more than 14,000 trees in 847 orchards across 17 cities. More than a million people live within walking distance of one. At a school near 80th and Main, students talked about eating fruit off the trees at lunch. The yearly harvest is described in the millions of pounds. This story stays with the Kansas City work and that national count. It does not list every other city.
kidQuestions: Why would a neighborhood plant fruit trees anyone can pick?
What would you need to do so a young orchard lasts?
How is a free orchard different from a grocery store?

kansas-city-go-baby-go.kidSummary: Nearly 100 high school robotics students from nine schools around Kansas City spent a Saturday adapting toy cars for toddlers who cannot get around the way their siblings can. They finished seven cars. A robotics coach said the point is to design with other people in mind. A parent said a car gives her child a way to move and play alongside siblings. Each car was fitted to a particular child rather than built from one template. The cars came from a children's charity. The students supplied the engineering.
kidQuestions: Why build each car for one child instead of making them all the same?
How does a ride-on car help a toddler play with siblings?
What would you change on a toy so more children could use it?

kearny-eagle-scout-glasses.kidSummary: Alexander Reis, a high school junior in Kearny, New Jersey, set out to collect 500 pairs of eyeglasses for his Eagle Scout project. Neighbors, schools, businesses, and a church brought in 3,673 pairs. The Lions Club will send them to people who need glasses. The project started close to home: a family member had lost his sight. Reis also hosted a community health fair, where nearly 45 people used a free vision screening. He said he had not pictured a goal of 500 pairs turning into thousands.
kidQuestions: Why are used eyeglasses still useful to someone else?
How did a family story shape the project Alexander chose?
What goal could your class set that neighbors might help you beat?

kingsford-playground-goal.kidSummary: Students at Kingsford Middle School in Michigan set out to raise $500 for a playground at Lake Antoine. They did not stop there. After the school had $3,800 with a day left, it raised the target to $5,000. By the end of Friday the students had brought in more than $8,000. An eighth grader said people kept giving after they thought $5,000 was the ceiling. With other community gifts, the full campaign passed the $40,000 it needed to finish the playground. A school drive that started small helped a park project cross the line.
kidQuestions: Why raise the goal when you are already close?
How can students raise money without it costing one family a lot?
What would you want a new playground to include?

klamath-chinook-return.kidSummary: Chinook salmon are swimming again in most of the Klamath River habitat that four dams blocked for about a hundred years. The dams came out in 2024. That fall, sonar counted 7,742 Chinook passing the old dam sites. In 2025 the count was more than 13,000. The fish reached 214 miles of river, about 88 percent of the places they used to live. Scientists said the speed surprised them. They also said a full comeback still depends on fish having young, and on water, habitat, and passage in the rest of the basin. The counts show a return. They are not a finished recovery.
kidQuestions: Why did dams stop salmon from reaching their old home waters?
What else has to go right before the salmon are truly back?
How do scientists count fish they cannot see one by one?

la-plata-childrens-books.kidSummary: Children waiting with their families at a social services office in La Plata, Maryland, can now read a book and take it home. The county library supplied about 100 children's books, in good condition, for a corner aimed at kids under 7. The office asked for books that would leave with children rather than stay in the waiting room. A library staff member said the point is to put stories in kids' hands outside a library building. Because the books are meant to go home, the library will keep restocking, and a volunteer group will add more titles.
kidQuestions: Why give the book away instead of asking a child to return it?
How can a story help during a long wait?
Where else, besides a library, should books be easy to find?

lincoln-banana-bread.kidSummary: Students in a life-skills program at the Rhode Island School for the Deaf bake banana bread for the Lincoln High football team before every game. The players met the bakers on the field ahead of a win, and the greeting has become part of how the two groups know each other. The bread shows up on game day. The meeting on the field is what turned a delivery into a friendship the team talks about. Deaf students and football players now share a tradition that started in a kitchen.
kidQuestions: How did a loaf of bread become a friendship?
What is a way to include someone who communicates differently from you?
What tradition could two groups at your school start together?

manchester-dahlias.kidSummary: Eighth graders at Maple Street School in Manchester, Vermont, spent an afternoon on a small kindness. They took dahlias from a local farm, before the first frost, made individual bouquets, and wrote notes to go with them. They walked to a grocery store and handed the flowers to employees and shoppers. People told the students the flowers had made their day. The paper described the walk as a lesson in empathy, not a fundraiser. The students found out what it feels like to do something small for a stranger and watch it land.
kidQuestions: Why can a flower and a note matter to someone at work?
How is this different from a fundraiser?
What small kindness could your class do on a walk through town?

medan-orangutan-return.kidSummary: A young male orangutan, about three years old, flew home to Sumatra after being rescued in India. He had been found in a cramped cage and cared for at a rescue center. Officials said this may be the first time a wild animal rescued in India has been sent back to the country it came from. He landed in Medan and will stay in quarantine, then move to a rehabilitation center in North Sumatra. Orangutans are protected by an international wildlife agreement. The landing starts that care. It is not a release into the forest yet.
kidQuestions: Why does a rescued orangutan need quarantine before meeting other animals?
Why is going back to Sumatra different from being set free in the forest?
What can people do so wild animals are not taken from their homes?

milford-teens-autism-kindness.kidSummary: Teenagers from Milford, Massachusetts, noticed 7-year-old Tristan Caron sitting by himself at an indoor play park in Bellingham and asked if he wanted to play. A short game of catch became about 40 minutes of hide-and-seek and time on the slide. His mother later found the teens so she could thank them. The teens said they had not known Tristan has autism. They saw a child on his own and wanted him in the game. One teen said she was glad he felt included. Another hoped people would think of that the next time someone is left out. The park plans a day to celebrate the teens.
kidQuestions: What did the teens notice before they knew anything else about Tristan?
How do you invite someone in without making a big show of it?
When have you seen someone left out, and what could you say?

montesano-opossums.kidSummary: Six baby opossums were too young to live on their own when an officer brought them to a wildlife center in Washington. The center raised them for several months. On October 3, the same officer helped release all six back into the wild in Montesano. The part worth telling is the ending. Six animals that arrived needing full-time care left able to go. A release is the goal of that kind of rescue: help, then let go.
kidQuestions: Why couldn't the baby opossums be released on the day they were found?
What does an animal need to learn before it can live outside?
How would you feel watching an animal you helped walk away?

mount-pleasant-meowdog-rescue.kidSummary: Students at Lucy Beckham High School in Mount Pleasant, South Carolina, help run an animal rescue at school. Their teacher started a veterinary science program, and the rescue takes dogs and cats from rural shelters. Students care for the animals, give medicine and vaccines with supervision, handle adoption paperwork, and help find foster and adoptive homes. One sophomore builds the rescue's website. A student described fostering a dog who had been considered for euthanasia and who now has a happy home. The rescue depends on donations and on fosters who take animals during school breaks.
kidQuestions: What jobs can students do for a rescue that adults usually do?
Why do the animals need foster homes when school is out?
Which part of this work would you want to try, and why?

nj-teens-financial-literacy-kits.kidSummary: Two high school seniors in New Jersey, Arjun Buch and Krishay Patel, noticed they had not learned much about money in elementary school. They built lesson kits for younger children. Each kit has a lesson and flash cards on needs versus wants, kinds of spending, and real-world problems such as a broken appliance. They started with workshops at libraries near Trenton, then expanded. They raised about $1,500 to make the first 1,000 kits and have placed them in 55 libraries across the state. They are still raising money to reach more libraries.
kidQuestions: What is the difference between a need and a want?
Why put money lessons in a library, where children already go?
What money question do you wish someone had explained earlier?

orange-county-olive-ridley.kidSummary: Biologists moved 204 olive ridley sea turtle eggs off beaches in Seal Beach and Huntington Beach, California. The nests, found in September, are the first known natural sea turtle nests on the U.S. West Coast. Storm surf and high tides were expected to wash them away. Teams packed the eggs in sand-filled coolers and drove them to an aquarium in Long Beach. They will sit in a quiet room for about 45 to 60 days. Nobody knows yet whether the eggs will hatch. If hatchlings do come out, the plan is to release them quickly so they still have energy to swim.
kidQuestions: Why move eggs instead of leaving them on the beach?
What could go wrong even after the eggs are safe in the aquarium?
Why might a turtle nest on a beach where nests had not been recorded before?

oregon-monarch-tags.kidSummary: At Blue Heron Park in Phoenix, Oregon, children and adults watched 22 monarch butterflies lift off wearing tiny solar tags. The tags weigh 60 milligrams, about a tenth of an adult monarch's weight, and a phone app can pick up the signal. One butterfly released in another Oregon town was detected a day later about 95 miles away, near the coast. A scientist had also tagged monarchs this year in several other Oregon cities, and about 100 more were released in Idaho. Roughly 200 people helped pay for the tags by adopting a butterfly. The tags draw a route people can follow.
kidQuestions: Why would scientists want to know where a monarch flies?
How can a tag that small stay on a butterfly?
What is one thing a garden can offer a monarch?

patton-pollinator-garden.kidSummary: Two Girl Scouts in Ebensburg, Pennsylvania, built a pollinator garden at Prince Gallitzin State Park. Makenna Sandoval and Lilly Prindle researched plants that grow naturally in the area and chose ones that flower from spring through fall, so different pollinators would have food across the seasons. They raised money, bought the plants, and put the garden in. Each girl logged more than 50 hours. They also made a flyer, coloring pages, a word search, and games the park can hand to visitors. A ribbon-cutting was held on September 20.
kidQuestions: Why does a pollinator garden need flowers in more than one season?
What is a pollinator, and why do people plant for them?
What would you put on a sign so visitors know how to help the garden?

roanoke-monarch-waystation.kidSummary: On a back lot in Roanoke, Virginia, weeds, privet, and trash cans used to fill the space. Jean Quade asked neighbors if she could dig up part of it. She thought she would plant a small section. The garden grew large enough to be certified as a Monarch Waystation, a public sign that it can feed monarchs on their migration. Neighbors who had not met before started pulling weeds, trading plants, and bringing children. One neighbor, 87, said the company matters to her. The gardens are for butterflies, and they have also become a place people know one another.
kidQuestions: What does a monarch need in a garden during migration?
How did a weedy lot turn into a place neighbors share?
What could your class plant that helps insects and people?

rutland-chestnut.kidSummary: Students at a school in Rutland, Vermont, have tended nine American chestnut trees for five years. They plant, fertilize, and spray to keep deer off. A blight found more than a hundred years ago nearly wiped this tree out of woods where it had been common. The point of the school grove is to keep the tree's genetics moving. Seeds from the grove have been planted at six other Vermont schools, and more trees have gone in around the city. It is a handful of trees, not a restored forest. It is a start that students can see from their own campus.
kidQuestions: Why does saving a few trees matter if a whole forest is gone?
What could students learn by caring for the same trees for years?
Why send seeds to other schools instead of keeping them all in one place?

seligman-black-footed-ferrets.kidSummary: Eighteen endangered black-footed ferrets were released near Seligman, Arizona, and six more went to Garland Prairie between Flagstaff and Williams. The animals flew in that day from a conservation center in Colorado. Before the release, the captive-born ferrets had survival training so they could hunt and look after themselves. The same day, the Phoenix Zoo said 34 kits had been born in seven litters, its best breeding year since 1999. Many of those kits will go to the national center for the same training before a later release. The department is also asking volunteers to help count ferrets with spotlights this fall.
kidQuestions: Why do ferrets born in care need training before they are set free?
What does a record number of kits make possible later?
How could a volunteer with a spotlight help scientists?

seward-barktoberfest.kidSummary: More than 20 dogs showed up in costume at a winery in Seward, Nebraska, for the third Barktoberfest. There was a pup-cup shuffle and a photo booth. The afternoon raises money for Blue River Pet Rescue, a foster-based group that opened in 2012 and finished its own building in 2019. The director said 2026 is a record year, with nearly 200 adoptions so far. One foster family is caring for a dog named Bunker, who came from Lexington. The costumes were the fun. The adoptions are the point of the day.
kidQuestions: Why do rescues need foster homes as well as a building?
What makes a costume party a useful way to help animals?
What would you want to know before adopting a dog?

sioux-falls-paint-plow.kidSummary: Sioux Falls, South Dakota, held Paint the Plow for the 17th year. More than 20 school and youth groups decorated city snowplows. People can vote for a favorite, and the winner rides in the Parade of Lights on November 27. The plows still have a winter job. For a few weeks they are also rolling art the students painted. A machine that usually clears streets became a canvas, and then it goes back to work.
kidQuestions: Why let students paint a machine the city uses for work?
How do you think the artists feel when their plow drives through town?
What everyday object in your town could use a student design?

springfield-go-baby-go.kidSummary: Families from around the Ozarks came to Missouri State University for free cars that help young children move. Occupational therapy students in Go Baby Go have done this for five years. About 30 families have taken part. Students add a go button so a child can move the car with their hands, plus side supports, a harness, and a switch so a parent can turn it off. One student said a child kept his hand on the button because he wanted to keep moving. Each car is a toy fitted to one child. It does not replace therapy.
kidQuestions: Why does a go button change who can drive the car?
Why build a switch a parent can use?
How is a toy built for one child different from a toy from a store shelf?

st-martinville-garden-day.kidSummary: More than 125 children spent a free day on a farm in St. Martinville, Louisiana, planting vegetables instead of sitting with screens. In the community garden they learned to put in carrots, turnips, potatoes, lettuce, and celery. Each child left with a cabbage started in a bucket. A teacher and a veterinarian talked with them about soil, animal health, and jobs in agriculture. The day also had hayrides, farm animals, and a pond. The foundation's first event drew 25 children. This one was the largest yet. The founder wants the farm to become a year-round place to learn about food and about giving away what you grow.
kidQuestions: What can you learn with your hands in a garden that a screen cannot show?
Why send every child home with a cabbage plant?
If your class grew food, who would you share it with?

stillwater-teddy-surgery.kidSummary: Oklahoma State University's veterinary school opened its doors and let families perform surgery on teddy bears. Children practiced the careful handling a vet student learns, on a stuffed patient that could not be hurt. One student now in the real program first tried it at the open house when they were 8. The bears are a way in. For at least one person, a stuffed-animal operation was the start of the training they are doing now. Play, done with care, can point toward a job.
kidQuestions: What can you practice on a teddy bear that you should not practice on a real animal?
Why might a childhood visit change what someone studies later?
What job would you want to try in a safe, pretend way first?

tallahassee-stuffed-animals.kidSummary: Kinsley Locke, a sophomore in Tallahassee, Florida, has spent about ten years collecting stuffed animals and giving them to fire departments in her county. She has now passed 2,000 donations, a project she calls Kinsley's Cuddles for Kids. She is widening the giving to children in foster care, and she hopes to donate another 1,000 stuffed animals this year. Firefighters often keep a plush toy for a child at a hard scene. The milestone is a long string of small comforts, counted one toy at a time.
kidQuestions: Why would a stuffed animal help a child who is scared?
What does it take to keep a project going for ten years?
What could you collect a little at a time for someone else?

thornton-nature-library.kidSummary: A library in Thornton, Colorado, lends the outdoors, not only books about it. Anythink Nature Library opened so people can check out books and borrow outdoor gear, or walk a trail on the open space just beyond the branch. The idea is that a camping trip or a hike should not depend on already owning the equipment. The library sits next to the land it wants people to use. A book can tell you about a trail. A borrowed pack can help you go.
kidQuestions: Why lend camping gear from a library?
What is something you would like to try outside if you could borrow the tools?
How is a trail outside a library different from a picture of a trail in a book?

tybee-loggerhead-nests.kidSummary: Loggerhead sea turtles nested on Tybee Island, Georgia, in numbers the island had not recorded before. Counters logged 59 nests, above the old high of 35 in 2022. The state of Georgia counted 4,292 nests this year, compared with a low of 384 in 2004. A team on Tybee moved 23 nests that sat too close to the water, including three emergency moves after waves uncovered eggs. The people who watch the beach link the rise to years of protection along the Georgia coast. The count is the good news: more mothers came ashore, and the work is showing up in the sand.
kidQuestions: Why move a nest that is too close to the waves?
What does a bigger nest count tell you about years of protection?
What should beach visitors do so they do not disturb a nest?

waco-duck-race.kidSummary: Eleven thousand rubber ducks went down the Brazos River in the Great Waco Duck Race. The race raises money for Dolly Parton's Imagination Library of Waco, which already mails one free book a month to more than 2,000 children in the county. The ducks are the fundraiser. The books are what the library sends home, a new one each month, for those children. A silly race on a river is how a town pays for something quiet: a book in a mailbox.
kidQuestions: How does a duck race turn into books for children?
Why might a free book every month matter more than one book once?
What silly event could your town hold to pay for something useful?

warren-giant-pumpkin.kidSummary: Ron Wallace of Greene, Rhode Island, grew a pumpkin that weighed 3,156 pounds at a weigh-off in Warren. That is nearly 300 pounds above the previous world record. The record is still pending official certification. A reading on the scale at a farm is not the last step. Until the group that keeps giant-pumpkin records certifies the weight, 3,156 pounds is the result announced at the weigh-off, not yet the formal world record. Wallace grew the pumpkin. The farm in Warren is where it was weighed, in front of people who came to see a vegetable the size of a small car.
kidQuestions: Why does a record need an official check after the scale reading?
What would a pumpkin that heavy need while it is growing?
What is something huge you have seen that started as a seed?

whitehall-bear-cub.kidSummary: A bear cub near Whitehall, Montana, had a plastic jar stuck on its head. Game wardens and a bear specialist caught the cub, cut the jar off, and let it go. The cub was not hurt. It went back to the woods without the jar. That was the whole job: notice the problem, remove it, and leave the animal wild. A jar that seems like trash to a person can become a trap for a curious cub.
kidQuestions: How can a plastic jar become dangerous for a wild animal?
Why let the cub go as soon as the jar was off?
What is one piece of trash you could keep from becoming a trap?

yellowstone-luna-terrier.kidSummary: Luna, a 10-year-old Jack Russell terrier, slipped out of a rented cabin at Canyon Village in Yellowstone on September 10. She had been a street dog in her first year, and those old habits made her hard to catch even after dozens of sightings. A trainer led the search. Permits were about to run out, and winter was closing in. On a Wednesday morning her family, back from California, found her inside a humane trap where she had been sleeping. She was in a small doghouse in the trap. She had lost about 10 pounds. They took her to a vet the same day.
kidQuestions: Why was Luna hard to catch even after people saw her?
What is a humane trap, and how is it different from a harmful one?
What should a family do if a pet gets lost in a wild park?
